h1:
Getting to Nan
flights, buses & mountain roads
intro: Nan sits deep in a valley in the far north of Thailand, so reaching it isn't as easy as Chiang Mai — but it's nowhere near as hard as you'd think. You can fly straight into the town, there are overnight buses, and once you arrive the town is small enough to explore by bicycle. The real draws like Pua, Bo Kluea and the sky road are further out, though, and you'll need your own wheels to get there. We've pulled together every option for you.

blocks.html: The first thing to get your head around before planning a Nan trip is that Nan has two very different zones. The first is Nan town — flat, small, and easy to spend a whole day exploring temples and cafes on foot or by bicycle. The other is the mountain side — Pua, Bo Kluea, Doi Phu Kha and the sky road — which sits 60–100 km from town along winding mountain roads and needs a car. So planning your trip really comes down to two questions: how do you get to Nan, and how do you get up the mountains once you're there?

The fastest way in is to fly. Nan Nakhon Airport (code NNT) is only about 3 km from the town centre, so a taxi or hotel shuttle gets you in within a few minutes. There are currently only a handful of direct Bangkok–Nan flights a day, mostly out of Don Mueang, taking around 1 hour 20 minutes. The two airlines on this route are Thai AirAsia and Nok Air, with one-way fares starting around 1,250–1,300 THB if you book ahead. Prices climb a lot during holidays and the peak cool season.

blocks.title: How to get a good fare
blocks.html: There are few flights to Nan and seats are limited, so prices jump fast as the date gets closer — especially in the cool season (Nov–Jan) when everyone heads to Nan. Booking 1–2 months ahead gets you a much better price, and it's worth comparing both airlines before you book.

items: From the airport into town — many hotels run shuttles, or you can grab a ride through an app or a taxi outside the terminal. It's a very short trip.

Pick up a hire car at the airport — some rental companies have a counter or will meet you at Nan Airport, so you can grab the car and head straight for the mountains. Handy if your main plan is Pua and Bo Kluea.
Flights can be delayed by the weather — some cool-season mornings get very foggy, so leave some buffer and don't schedule anything tight for your arrival day.

blocks.html: If you're not in a rush and want to save money, the overnight bus is a popular option. They leave Mo Chit 2 bus terminal in the evening and arrive in Nan the next morning, taking around 10–11 hours. The main operators on this route are Sombat Tour and Nakhonchai Air, including VIP coaches with wide reclining seats. Fares vary by class, roughly 500–750 THB one way. An overnight departure makes the best use of your time since you sleep on the bus and wake up right as you arrive.

blocks.title: Riding the overnight bus comfortably
blocks.html: Pick a VIP or first-class coach if you find it hard to sleep, because the Bangkok–Nan route is long and the last stretch is winding mountain road. Bring a warm layer on board too — the air-con on these buses is usually freezing.

blocks.text: From Chiang Mai and other northern towns

blocks.html: Plenty of people are already in Chiang Mai and tack Nan onto the trip. The Chiang Mai–Nan route has both minivans and buses, taking around 6 hours, and it's mountain road almost the whole way — bring something if you get carsick. If you'd rather drive your own hire car from Chiang Mai you can; it's about 300 km, a relaxed 5–6 hours including stops. There are also easy connections from Phrae, Phayao and Den Chai, since Nan is where several routes come together.

items.name: Chiang Mai → Nan
items.blurb: Minivan or bus around 6 hrs, mountain road the whole way, or self-drive around 300 km with a stop in Phrae along the way.

items.name: Phrae / Den Chai → Nan
items.blurb: The closest, around 2 hrs. Good if you take the train to Den Chai and connect onward into Nan.

items.name: Phayao → Nan
items.blurb: Around 2.5–3 hrs, links a Phayao–Nan trip nicely. A quiet road with good views.

blocks.text: Car and motorbike hire in Nan

blocks.html: Once you're in Nan, you'll need your own wheels to explore the mountain side, because public transport up to Pua and Bo Kluea is limited and inflexible. Nan town has several rental shops, both self-drive and with a driver. A small sedan like a Yaris or City starts around 670–800 THB a day, with bigger cars costing more by model, and some shops charge extra if you drive out of the province. Motorbike hire starts around 200–300 THB a day, good for getting around town and the nearby areas.

blocks.title: Check the vehicle before driving the mountains
blocks.html: If your plan is Bo Kluea, Doi Phu Kha and the 1256 sky road, pick a car with enough power, because the roads are steep with lots of curves. A 110–125cc motorbike can struggle on long steep climbs, so if you're not used to mountain riding a car is safer. Always check the brakes and tyres before you take the vehicle.

items: Bring your driving licence + ID card / passport — most shops ask for a copy or a deposit.
Photograph the vehicle before you take it — existing scratches, fuel level and the odometer, to avoid disputes when you return it.
Ask about insurance — check what it actually covers, especially if you'll be driving in the mountains.
Fill up before heading into the mountains — petrol stations on the Bo Kluea–Doi Phu Kha route are far apart, so top up in town or in Pua first.

blocks.html: One of Nan's charms is that the town is small, flat and not crowded with traffic, which makes it the most relaxing place to explore by bicycle. Key temples like Wat Phumin, the Khuang Mueang square and the Nan National Museum are all within a few minutes of each other, so half a day of cycling around the old town covers almost everything. The mood is laid-back, and it suits slowly taking the town in far more than driving past it.

items: Where to borrow or rent a bike — many hotels and guesthouses in the old town lend bicycles for free or rent them cheaply, and some have them specifically for guests.
Nan Municipality Tourist Information Centre — on Pha Kong Road, a good starting point with route information and old-town maps.
The popular loop — Wat Phumin → Khuang Mueang → the museum → Wat Phra That Chang Kham, then loop back to a cafe in the old town.
Ride in the morning or evening — midday sun is harsh, while early mornings have nice weather and emptier streets.

blocks.title: Easy in town, but don't push it on the mountains
blocks.html: Bicycles are for the town only — don't even think about cycling up to Pua or Bo Kluea. It's far and very steep. For the mountain side, use a car or a motorbike with enough power.

blocks.text: Driving up to Pua, Bo Kluea, Doi Phu Kha and the 1256 sky road

blocks.html: This is the highlight most people come to Nan for, but it's also the part that needs the most planning, because it's far out and all mountain road. From Nan town to Pua district is about 60 km, just over an hour on a good road. From Pua up to Doi Phu Kha National Park is another 25 km or so, and getting to Bo Kluea via the 1256 sky road is around 50 km further on from Pua — gorgeous winding road along the ridge. That's a lot of driving in one day, so we'd suggest staying a night in Pua or Bo Kluea so you're not rushing.

items: The main route — Nan town → Pua (Route 1080) → Doi Phu Kha / → Bo Kluea via the 1256 sky road, with stretches of beautiful mountain and mist views.
Leave early — if you want to do Pua–Bo Kluea as a day return you need an early start, because driving mountain roads at night is dangerous.
Watch for slippery roads in the rainy season — Jun–Oct rain makes the roads slick and brings fog, so drive slowly, use your lights and keep your distance.
The cool season is busy — Nov–Jan has the best views but the most traffic, and accommodation in Pua and Bo Kluea fills up fast, so book ahead.

blocks.title: Budget extra time for the mountains
blocks.html: Distances may not look far on the map, but the winding climbs and descents take longer than you'd expect. Don't pack the plan so tight that you're rushing — driving mountain roads in the dark or rain is far riskier, so always plan to reach your accommodation before nightfall.

faq.q: Which airport do you fly into for Nan, and how long does it take?
faq.a: You fly into Nan Nakhon Airport (NNT), only about 3 km from the town centre. There are a handful of direct flights a day from Bangkok (Don Mueang) with Thai AirAsia and Nok Air, taking around 1 hour 20 minutes. One-way fares start around 1,250 THB if you book ahead.

faq.q: How many hours is the bus from Bangkok to Nan?
faq.a: Around 10–11 hours. Buses leave Mo Chit 2 in the evening and arrive in Nan the next morning. The main operators are Sombat Tour and Nakhonchai Air, with comfortable VIP coaches, and fares run about 500–750 THB depending on the class.

faq.q: Do you need to hire a car in Nan?
faq.a: If you're only exploring the old town, no — you can comfortably cycle or walk to the temples and cafes. But if you want to head up to Pua, Bo Kluea, Doi Phu Kha or the 1256 sky road, you'll need your own wheels, because public transport up the mountains is limited and inflexible.

faq.q: How much does car hire cost in Nan?
faq.a: A small sedan starts around 670–800 THB a day, with bigger cars costing more by model, and motorbikes from around 200–300 THB a day. Some shops charge extra if you drive out of the province. For the mountains, go for a car with enough power, since the roads are steep with lots of curves.

faq.q: How far is the drive from Nan town to Pua and Bo Kluea?
faq.a: From Nan town to Pua is about 60 km, just over an hour. From Pua up to Doi Phu Kha is another 25 km or so, and Bo Kluea via the 1256 sky road is around 50 km further on from Pua, all winding mountain road. We'd suggest staying a night in Pua or Bo Kluea so you're not rushing.
